newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE Euroyen futures ease, overnight rate jumps.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE Euroyen futures ease, overnight rate jumps.

text.p: The key December three-month Euroyen deposit rate futures contract closed easier on Thursday following Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments implying the possibility of higher U.S. interest rates.

But the contract's fall was limited because traders said a change in monetary policy in Japan was far less likely than in the U.S. Meanwhile, the short-end key overnight interbank rate jumped to its highest level since April 3, 1996.

Traders said some banks which were in a hurry to raise funds at the short end of the market were to blame for the rise in the key overnight rate. It was mainly traded at 0.53 percent on Thursday, up from Wednesday's weighted average of 0.51.

After the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) morning operation, which some said was less generous than expected, a view emerged, albeit briefly, that the BOJ might let the key overnight rate rise before confirming any policy change in an announcement.
But such a view withered as many believe a rise in rates is unlikely unless Japan's bad loan problems are solved or its economic recovery is unhurt by fiscal tightening from April.
A dealer at long-term credit bank said: "Many people did not see today's operation as a step torward higher interest rates. So the downside room for the key December contract was limited."

The fall was also limited by a forecast fall in Japan's February and March industrial output, traders said. The Trade Ministry forecast that manufacturers' output will decrease 3.3 percent month-on-month in February and by 2.7 percent in March.
The key December contract settled down 0.02 at 99.23. It moved from 99.22 to 99.24 with 28,365 contracts changing hands.

Given a view that the BOJ will try to keep the key overnight call below 0.50 percent in the near future, banks prefered raising funds at the short-end of the market, although traders said demand was rising ahead of the fiscal year-end.

The BOJ continued to supply sufficient funds to offset a market shortage in the morning, but set repurchase agreements of the offered bills and T-bills within this fiscal year. Traders said those who did not expect this pushed the key overnight rate as high as 0.55 percent.
A BOJ official said the rate's rise was due to seasonal fund demand ahead of the end of the month.

In the longer-term cash market, the one-month certificates of deposit (CD) rate rose to 0.55 percent. The one-month CDs to be settled on March 3 are the first such CDs to cover fiscal book closings, traders said.
The CDs were last issued at 0.52 percent on February 10.
Neither two- nor three-month CDs were issued on Thursday, but they were both offered at 0.54 percent, unchanged from previously issued levels.
